title: Adab with the earth
hook: the end of the world arrives, and there's a seedling in your hand

segments.voice: Yesterday: adab with creation, from the cat shut in to the dog at the well. Today, the ground they all stand on, which day six hundred eighty-four asked us not to spoil.

The Hour has come. The end of everything. And there you are, holding a small palm shoot, roots still in a clump of soil. What now? The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, answered that exact question. In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, in paraphrase: if the Hour is established and one of you has a seedling in his hand, and he is able to plant it before he stands up, let him plant it.
screen: `THE HOUR HAS COME.` → `A SEEDLING IN YOUR HAND.` → `PLANT IT.`

segments.voice: Sit with how strange that is. If the world is ending, nobody will eat the dates or rest in the shade. And still: plant it. The hadith pulls the act loose from its result. Then the Qur'an gives the reason the earth is in our hands at all. Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." Khalifa: a deputy, a steward, someone looking after what belongs to another. In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, the Prophet adds: the world is sweet and green, and Allah has made you successors in it, to see how you act. Stewards are watched for how they treat the estate. Then a hadith that turns the garden into worship. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: whenever a Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop, and a bird, or a person, or an animal eats from it, it counts as charity for him. By that hadith, even the sparrow that steals your figs leaves a charity behind. So the adab with the earth comes down to three movements. Plant, even when you won't see the fruit. Look after it as a steward, not an owner. And let the birds have their share. That closes the manners of daily life, down to the soil underfoot. Tomorrow the path turns inward, to the virtues.
screen: `PLANT IT, EVEN AT THE END.` · `A VICEROY IN THE EARTH.` · `SWEET AND GREEN, AND WATCHED.` · `THE BIRD'S SHARE IS CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Feel your weight resting on the ground, or on a floor built on the ground, and bring to mind one small patch of earth you can reach: a pot on the windowsill, a yard, a crack in the sidewalk where something is already trying. Picture putting something into it, a seed, a cutting, or water for a thirsty plant, and notice you don't need to see it grow. If you pray, you can offer that small planting with the remembrance of Allah.
Adab with the earth. The manners of a steward: planting even when you won't see the fruit, looking after what was entrusted, and letting the birds have their share. Today's word.
Your line: plant it anyway. The birds get their share too. That's day one thousand three hundred five.

howItsDone: Islamic teaching on the earth draws on the Qur'an's description of humanity as khalifa, a steward on the earth, and on hadith that count planting as charity and that urge planting a seedling even when the Hour comes.

chat.says: If the world might end soon, why bother planting anything?
options: The Prophet said if the Hour comes with a seedling in your hand, plant it anyway.
Only plant what you'll harvest yourself; the earth is ours to use up.
Planting is good, but it only counts if a person eats the fruit.
chat.meaning: The hadith says plant even at the Hour, and in Bukhari, whatever a bird, person or animal eats from your planting counts as charity.
